title: Plan and post weekly social content
purpose: Keeps your business visible with a steady, planned stream of useful posts instead of last-minute scrambling. Done means a week of posts is written, scheduled, published, and checked for what worked.
tools: Social platforms; Scheduling tool; Calendar; Notes or document
steps: ## Plan the week
Block [30 minutes] on [day of the week] for planning. Put it in your calendar as a repeating appointment so it happens even when the week is busy.
Choose one theme for the week. Pick something tied to a service you offer or a question clients ask often, such as [your main offer] or [a common client question].
List [3 to 5] posts that support the theme. Mix teaching, a client story or result (with permission), a behind-the-scenes moment, and one clear invitation to [your call to action].
Check your calendar for launches, holidays, and events. Add a post to promote [upcoming event or offer] so nothing important is missed.
## Create and schedule
Write all of the week's posts in one sitting. Open your notes document and draft each caption in your own voice, short and specific, with one idea per post.
Add an image, graphic, or short video to each post. Use your [brand colors and fonts] and keep a folder of reusable templates so this takes minutes, not hours.
Add a clear next step to each post. Link to [your booking link or sign-up page] or invite replies with a simple question.
Schedule every post in your scheduling tool. Set times when your audience is usually online, such as [best posting times for your audience].
## Post and review
Reply to comments and messages within [one business day]. Answer questions, thank people by name, and note any message that sounds like a possible new client.
Move interested people into your CRM or contact list. Add their name, where they found you, and a note of what they asked about.
Review results at the end of the week. Note which [2 posts] got the most replies, saves, or clicks and write down one thing to repeat next week.
Confirm next week's planning block is on your calendar. Done looks like posts scheduled, replies answered, and one lesson noted.

title: Send a weekly email newsletter
purpose: Keeps you in regular, useful contact with your audience and past clients so you are the first name they think of. Done means an issue is written, tested, sent on schedule, and its results noted.
tools: Email; Email list or CRM; Calendar; Notes or document
steps: ## Prepare
Set a fixed send day and time of [day] at [time]. Consistency matters more than perfection, so choose a slot you can keep for months.
Keep a running ideas list in one place. Add questions clients ask, wins, tips, and upcoming dates as they come up so you never start from a blank page.
Pick one main topic for this issue. Choose something useful to your readers, such as [a tip, a story, or the answer to a common question].
Gather any links, images, or dates you need. Have [your booking link] and any event or offer details ready before you start writing.
## Write and check
Write the subject line first. Keep it under about [50 characters], plain and specific, and say what the reader will get from opening it.
Draft the body in a friendly voice, as if writing to one person. Aim for [300 to 500 words]: a short opening, one useful idea, and one clear next step.
Add one call to action. Use a single link or reply request, for example [book a call, read the full article, or reply with a question].
Send a test to yourself and read it on your phone. Check links, spelling, your name, and that nothing looks cut off or out of order.
Confirm the list is current. Make sure people who have unsubscribed are removed and that the right [list or segment] is selected.
## Send and follow up
Schedule or send the issue at your set time. Double-check that the sender name and reply-to address are the ones you want clients to answer.
Reply personally to anyone who responds. Aim to answer within [one business day] and note any replies that show interest in working with you.
Record the results in your notes. Write down the open rate, clicks, and unsubscribes, plus the one topic that drew the most interest.
Add next week's topic to your ideas list. Done looks like the issue sent, replies answered, and the next topic chosen.

title: Run a free webinar or workshop
purpose: Gives potential clients a low-risk way to experience your expertise and take a clear next step. Done means the event ran smoothly, attendees received the replay and follow-up, and interested people are in your pipeline.
tools: Webinar or video meeting tool; Email; Calendar; Landing page or form; CRM
steps: ## Plan and promote
Define one promise for the session. Write a single sentence: who it is for and what they will be able to do by the end, such as [specific outcome for your ideal client].
Choose a date, start time, and length. Pick a time that suits your audience, plan for [45 to 60 minutes], and add a preparation block to your calendar.
Create a simple sign-up page or form. Include the promise, date, time zone, and a button to register at [your registration link].
Send an invitation to your list and post about it. Plan [three reminders]: when you open registration, one week before, and one day before.
Set up a confirmation and reminder email. Include the join link, what to bring, and how to reach you if they cannot attend live.
## Prepare and run
Outline the session in three parts. Plan an opening, [2 to 3 teaching points] with one example each, and a closing with your offer.
Do a technical check one day before. Test your camera, microphone, slides, and the join link, and have a backup way to reach attendees such as email.
Start on time and set expectations. Welcome people, say how long the session will run, and tell them when you will take questions.
Present your next step once, clearly. Offer [your free call, program, or resource] and share the link in the chat or on screen.
Record the session if you have permission. Tell attendees at the start that it is being recorded and how you will use it.
## Follow up
Send the replay and any resources within [24 hours]. Thank attendees and no-shows alike, and repeat your single next step with [your booking link].
Add attendees to your CRM or contact list. Tag each person as attended, no-show, or asked a question, and note what they said they need.
Reach out personally to the most engaged people. Send a short message to anyone who asked a question or stayed to the end.
Review what worked. Note attendance, replies, and bookings, plus one change for next time. Done looks like follow-up sent and every attendee in your list.

title: Publish a blog post or article
purpose: Builds trust and helps the right people find you by sharing useful, searchable knowledge. Done means a clear, checked article is published, shared, and recorded in your content list.
tools: Website or blog editor; Document editor; Image tool; Email; Social platforms
steps: ## Plan the post
Choose one question your ideal client asks. Write it as the working title, for example [a question you hear on calls].
Name the reader and the goal. Write one line: who this is for and what they should understand or do after reading.
List three to five key points. Use real examples from your work, with names and details removed or approved by [the client].
Pick a short phrase people might search for. Use it in the title, the opening, and one heading, and keep the wording natural.
## Write and edit
Write a rough draft without editing as you go. Aim for [800 to 1,200 words] in plain language, with short paragraphs and clear subheadings.
Open with the problem and close with a next step. End with one invitation to [book a call, join your list, or download a resource].
Let the draft rest, then edit. Cut anything that does not help the reader, shorten long sentences, and read it aloud once to catch awkward lines.
Check facts, claims, and links. Confirm any statistic or quote has a source, and have [a professional in your field] review anything that gives specialist advice.
## Publish and share
Add a title, image, and short summary in your editor. Write a description of about [150 characters] and add descriptive text to the image.
Preview on your phone and computer. Check headings, links, and that the call to action button works before you publish.
Publish and share it in three places. Post to [your social platforms], send it to your email list, and mention it in your next conversation where it fits.
Add the post to your content list. Record the title, date, link, and topic, and set a date in [30 days] to check views and inquiries.

title: Run a paid ad campaign
purpose: Puts a specific offer in front of the right people on a budget you control, and tracks whether it brings in leads worth the cost. Done means the campaign is live, monitored, and reviewed against a number you set in advance.
tools: Ad platform; Landing page or form; Spreadsheet; CRM; Calendar
steps: ## Set up the campaign
Write down one goal and one number. For example, [number of leads] at no more than [cost per lead] over [number of days].
Set a budget you can comfortably afford. Choose a daily and total limit of [amount], and check with your [accountant] if you are unsure how it fits your finances.
Define your audience in one sentence. Name location, role or situation, and interests, such as [your ideal client description].
Build a landing page or form for a single action. Make sure it matches the ad message and includes [your offer and sign-up form].
Write two versions of the ad. Change only one thing, such as the headline or image, so you can see which one works better.
Add tracking before you launch. Confirm that form submissions and bookings are recorded and that leads arrive in your CRM or contact list.
## Launch and monitor
Check every ad, link, and form before you switch it on. Click through as a visitor, submit a test entry, and confirm you receive it.
Check results daily for the first [three days]. Look at spend, clicks, and leads, and pause anything that is spending with no response.
Reply to new leads within [one business day]. Fast follow-up is usually what turns a paid lead into a conversation.
Hold changes until you have enough data. Wait for about [a week or a set number of clicks] before editing so you are not guessing.
## Review and decide
Compare results to the goal you wrote down. Record total spend, leads, booked calls, and new clients in your spreadsheet.
Decide to stop, adjust, or continue. Keep the better ad, retire the weaker one, and write down what you will test next.
Store what you learned. Note the audience, message, and cost per lead in [your marketing notes] so the next campaign starts ahead. Done looks like a decision recorded.

title: Attend or host a networking event
purpose: Helps you meet potential clients and referral partners in person or online and turn conversations into real follow-up. Done means each useful contact is recorded and has received a personal message within two days.
tools: Calendar; Contact list or CRM; Email; Notes; Business cards or digital card
steps: ## Before the event
Decide why you are going. Write one goal, such as [meet 3 potential clients or 2 referral partners], so you know when it went well.
Check who is attending. Review the guest list or host page and note [3 people or types of people] you would like to meet.
Prepare a short introduction. Write one or two sentences covering who you help, with what, and the result, such as [your one-line introduction].
Pack what you need. Bring [business cards or your digital contact link], a pen, and your phone with a notes app ready.
## At the event
Arrive early and start with one person. Early arrivals are easier to talk to, and a first conversation makes it easier to join groups later.
Ask questions and listen. Find out what the other person does and what would make their week easier before you talk about your work.
Take a quick note after each useful conversation. Write the name, what you discussed, and any promised next step so you do not rely on memory.
Offer something helpful, not a pitch. Share an introduction, a resource, or an idea, and invite a follow-up conversation only if there is a fit.
## After the event
Add every new contact to your CRM or contact list within [24 hours]. Include where you met, what you discussed, and a tag for follow-up.
Send a personal message within [two business days]. Mention something specific from your conversation and suggest one next step such as [a coffee or a call].
Do what you said you would do. Send the introduction, link, or resource you promised and tick it off your list.
Rate the event in your notes. Record cost, contacts made, and conversations that led somewhere, then decide whether to attend again.

title: Build and maintain partner and collaborator relationships
purpose: Builds a small network of trusted people and businesses who send you referrals and whom you can support in return. Done means partners are listed, contacted on a regular schedule, and thanked for every introduction.
tools: CRM or contact list; Email; Calendar; Spreadsheet
steps: ## Choose and list your partners
Make a list of people your ideal clients already trust. Think of [types of businesses or professionals] who serve the same people without competing with you.
Pick your top [5 to 10] to focus on first. Choose people you know and respect, and whose clients would benefit from what you do.
Record each partner in your CRM or contact list. Add their name, business, what they do, how you met, and the kind of client they could refer.
Write one clear sentence describing a good referral for you. Share it so partners know exactly what to say, such as [your ideal referral description].
## Stay in touch
Set a regular contact rhythm. Plan to reach each partner at least [once every 6 to 8 weeks] and add the reminders to your calendar.
Contact them with something of value, not a request. Share an article, make an introduction, or send a note about something they did well.
Offer a short catch-up conversation each quarter. Use it to learn about their current goals and tell them what you are working on.
Keep a note of what each partner needs. Track their goals and ideal clients so you can refer people to them in return.
## Review and thank
Thank each partner within [one business day] of any referral. Send a personal note or [a small gift]. If you plan to pay referral fees, check the rules for your field with your [attorney] first.
Tell the partner what happened, where appropriate. Share the outcome while respecting the client's privacy and any agreement you have.
Review your partner list every [quarter]. Note who referred whom, who has gone quiet, and who you want to build a stronger connection with.
Update your list and calendar. Done looks like every partner with a next contact date and every recent referral acknowledged.

title: Respond to a new lead within one hour
purpose: Speed is the strongest signal that you are easy to work with. This process makes sure every new inquiry gets a warm, personal reply within one hour during [business hours] and a clear next step.
tools: Email; Phone or text; CRM or contact list; Calendar; Notifications
steps: ## Be ready to respond
Turn on notifications for new inquiries. Send form submissions, messages, and calls to [your phone or email] so you see them quickly.
Save a reply template for each common inquiry. Write short, warm drafts with blanks for the name and question, and keep them where you can reach them fast.
Decide who responds and when. Name a backup for [times you are unavailable] so no lead waits more than one hour during business hours.
## Reply within the hour
Read the whole inquiry before you reply. Note their name, what they asked, and anything urgent or unclear.
Use their name and answer their actual question first. Then say one sentence about how you can help and what happens next.
Offer one clear next step. Share [your booking link] for a call, or ask one simple question if you need more detail.
Reply in the same way they contacted you. Answer email with email, and use text or a call if they gave a phone number and asked for that.
Check your message before sending. Confirm spelling, the name, the link, and that the tone is friendly and not pushy.
## Follow up and record
Add the lead to your CRM or contact list right away. Record name, contact details, source, date, and what they asked for.
Set a follow-up reminder for [two business days]. If they have not replied, send a short, kind check-in with the same link.
Continue [three follow-ups over two weeks], then stop. After that, move them to a longer-term list and tell them they are welcome to reach out later.
Review your response times weekly. Done looks like every lead replied to within an hour and logged with a next action.

title: Run a discovery or sales call
purpose: Helps you understand what a prospect really needs, decide honestly whether you can help, and agree a clear next step. Done means the call is held, notes are recorded, and the next step is confirmed in writing.
tools: Calendar; Video meeting tool or phone; CRM or contact list; Notes; Email
steps: ## Prepare
Review what you know about the person [15 minutes] before the call. Read their form answers, messages, and any website or profile they shared.
Write three goals for the call. Aim to understand their situation, decide whether you are a good fit, and agree a next step.
List your key questions. Prepare [five to seven] open questions about their goals, what they have tried, what is in the way, and what success looks like.
Set up your space and tools. Test your audio and video, close other windows, and have your notes and [your pricing outline] ready.
## During the call
Open warmly and set the plan. Say how long you have, what you will cover, and that you will leave time for their questions.
Ask your questions and listen more than you talk. Let them finish, take brief notes, and repeat back what you heard to confirm it.
Find out what happens if nothing changes. Ask about timing, budget range, and who else is involved in the decision.
Explain how you would help in plain language. Link your approach directly to what they told you, and share [your price or range] if appropriate.
Be honest if it is not a good fit. Recommend someone else or another route, which builds trust and saves you both time.
Agree the next step before you end. Confirm what happens, who does it, and by when, such as [sending a proposal or booking a start date].
## After the call
Write your notes within [15 minutes]. Record their goals, concerns, budget, timeline, and the agreed next step in your CRM or contact list.
Send a thank-you email the same day. Summarize the next step, include any promised link or resource, and keep it short.
Set a follow-up reminder in your calendar. Done looks like notes saved, the email sent, and a dated next action.

title: Send a proposal or quote
purpose: Turns a good conversation into a clear, written offer the client can say yes to with confidence. Done means a complete proposal is checked, sent within [one business day] of the call, and followed up on a set schedule.
tools: Document editor; Email; E-signature or approval method; Invoicing tool; CRM
steps: ## Prepare the proposal
Review your notes from the conversation. Pull out their goals, challenges, timeline, and the exact words they used to describe success.
Start from your saved proposal template. Add their name, the date, and a short summary of what they told you they need.
Describe the work in plain terms. List what you will do, what they will receive, how long it takes, and what you need from them.
State the price and what it includes. Show [your price or options], the payment schedule, and anything that is not included to prevent surprises.
Add your terms. Include dates, changes, cancellations, and payment due dates, and have your [attorney] review your standard terms.
Give the proposal an expiry date, for example [14 days from sending], so there is a gentle reason to decide.
## Send and follow up
Check the proposal before you send it. Read it as the client, and confirm the name, prices, dates, and spelling are correct.
Send it within [one business day] of the conversation. Attach it to a short, warm email and offer a quick call to go through any questions.
Log it in your CRM or contact list. Record the date sent, the amount, and the expiry date.
Follow up on [day 3 and day 7]. Ask if they have questions, and offer to adjust anything that is in the way of a yes.
## Close the loop
When they say yes, confirm the details in writing. Send [your agreement and first invoice] through your invoicing tool, and set the start date.
When they say no or not yet, ask what would help. Thank them, note the reason in your CRM or contact list, and set a reminder to check back in [3 months].
Update your proposal template with anything you improved. Done looks like every sent proposal tracked to a clear yes, no, or dated follow-up.

title: Follow up with leads who have gone quiet
purpose: Leads often go quiet because life got busy, not because they said no. This process gives every quiet lead a short, respectful follow-up sequence and a clear final status, so no opportunity is left sitting without a decision.
tools: CRM or contact list; Email; Calendar; Phone or text
steps: ## Find who has gone quiet
Filter your CRM or contact list for leads with no reply in [7] days. Include anyone who had a call, proposal or quote but did not answer your last message.
Sort the list from warmest to coldest. Put people who asked for pricing or booked a call at the top, and general inquiries at the bottom.
Reread the last conversation with each lead before you write. Note what they asked for, what worried them, and anything you promised to send.
Remove anyone who said no, asked you to stop, or has already bought. Following up with them damages trust.
## Send the follow-up sequence
Send a short check-in on day [7]. Mention something specific from your last conversation and ask one easy question, such as 'Is this still something you want to move on?'
Send a helpful message on day [14]. Share one useful item, such as [a case study, short guide or answer to their question], with no request attached.
Send a direct message on day [21]. Offer two clear options: book a call at [your booking link], or tell you the timing is not right.
Try a second channel if email gets no reply. A short text or phone call from [your phone number] works well, but only use channels the lead has already used with you.
Log every message in your CRM the same day. Record the date, the channel and what you said so you never repeat yourself.
## Close the loop
Send a final polite note on day [28]. Say you will stop reaching out and that they can contact you any time at [your email].
Move non-responders to a 'Not now' list. Add them to [your newsletter or update list] only if they agreed to receive it.
Set a reminder to review the 'Not now' list in [90] days. A reply then often arrives when circumstances have changed.
Check that every quiet lead has a logged next step, a reminder or a closed status. Done means nothing is left without a decision.

title: Close the sale and collect payment
purpose: This process turns a yes into a signed agreement and received payment, with no confusion about what was bought. Done means the agreement is signed, payment has cleared, the record is updated and the client knows what happens next.
tools: CRM or contact list; Email; Invoicing tool; Agreement or e-signature tool
steps: ## Confirm the decision
Review the lead's notes before you reach out. Check what they want, their budget, and any question you promised to answer.
Ask for the decision in plain words. For example: 'Based on what we discussed, would you like to move forward with [your offer name]?' Then stop talking and let them answer.
Restate what they are getting. Name the outcome, what is included, the timeline and the price of [your price] so nothing is a surprise later.
Answer any final question briefly and honestly. If you need time to check, give a specific time you will reply by.
## Collect agreement and payment
Send the agreement the same day. Use your [agreement template] and include scope, price, payment terms and start date. Have your [attorney] review the template before you first use it.
Send the invoice or payment link with the agreement. Use [your invoicing tool] and state the amount, due date and accepted payment methods in the message.
Offer a payment plan only if you already have one set up. State the exact schedule from [your payment plan options] so there is no back and forth.
Confirm payment has cleared before you begin work. Open your invoicing tool, check that the status shows paid, and note the date in your CRM.
Send a receipt or payment confirmation within [one business day]. Include the amount, the date and what it covers.
Send a friendly reminder on day [3] if payment is late, and a firmer one on day [7]. Hold the start date until payment or a payment plan is in place.
## Wrap up the sale
Update the contact in your CRM to 'Client'. Record the offer, price, payment date and start date.
Send a short thank you with the next step. Say what happens next and when, and include [your booking link or onboarding form].
Pass the signed agreement, call notes and payment record to whoever runs onboarding. Done means nothing needs to be asked of the client twice.

title: Handle objections on a sales call
purpose: Objections are usually questions in disguise. This process helps you prepare honest answers, respond calmly on the call, and learn from every objection so your offer and conversations improve over time.
tools: Notes document; CRM or contact list; Calendar; Phone or video call
steps: ## Prepare before the call
List the [5] objections you hear most often. Common ones are price, timing, trust, 'I need to think about it' and 'I need to ask my partner'. Keep the list where you can see it during calls.
Write one honest answer for each objection in your own words. Base it on a real result, fact or policy, not a pressure line.
Choose one or two short client stories to use as proof, such as [client result or testimonial]. Remove names unless you have written permission to share them.
Decide your limits in advance. Know what you can offer on price, payment plans or timing, and what you will not change.
## During the call
Let them finish before you respond. Count to two after they stop speaking. Interrupting makes the concern feel dismissed.
Repeat the concern back in your own words. For example: 'So the main worry is whether this fits your budget this quarter. Is that right?'
Ask one question to find the real reason. Try 'What would need to be true for this to feel like a yes?' Many objections cover a different concern.
Answer the concern directly and briefly. Use your prepared answer, then ask 'Does that address it?' before moving on.
Offer proof, not pressure. Share a relevant story or fact and let them decide. Never invent deadlines or urgency that is not real.
Accept a no gracefully. If the fit is wrong, say so kindly and offer [a lower-cost option, a resource or a referral].
## After the call
Write down each objection and your answer in your CRM within [one hour]. Note whether it was resolved.
Send a follow-up within [24 hours]. Answer anything left open and include the next step, such as [your booking link].
Review the objections you logged once a month. If one keeps appearing, adjust your offer, your page or your early conversations to address it.

title: Keep the pipeline clean each week
purpose: A tidy pipeline shows you where your next clients are and stops leads from slipping away. Done means every open lead has a stage, a next step and a date, and you know your weekly numbers.
tools: CRM or contact list; Calendar; Notes document
steps: ## Set up your weekly review
Block [30 minutes] on [the same day each week]. Make it a repeating calendar event and treat it like a client appointment.
Open your CRM or contact list to the full pipeline view. Make sure you can see every stage and the date of each lead's last activity.
Open your notes from the past week's calls and messages. Anything not yet logged gets logged first.
## Clean up each stage
Update any lead whose status has changed. Move people to the stage that reflects what really happened, not what you hope will happen.
Find leads with no activity in [14] days. For each one, choose: follow up today, set a date to follow up, or close it out.
Give every open lead a next step and a date. A lead with no next action is the most common way deals quietly disappear.
Close out leads that are finished. Mark them lost, record the reason in one line, and remove them from your active view.
Fix duplicates and missing details. Check names, emails, phone numbers and where each lead came from.
Check the value on each open deal. Make sure the amount still matches what you have discussed with them.
## Plan the week ahead
Count the leads in each stage and compare with last week. Write down new leads, calls booked, proposals sent and sales closed.
Pick the [3] leads most likely to close this week. Put a specific follow-up for each one on your calendar.
Write down one thing to improve, such as a stage where leads get stuck or a source that brings few good leads.
Save your numbers in [your tracking sheet or notes]. Done means next week's review starts from a clean list.

title: Onboard a new client from welcome to first session
purpose: A smooth start builds trust and sets the tone for the whole engagement. This process takes a new client from payment to a well-prepared first session, with every form, date and expectation in place.
tools: Email; Calendar; CRM or contact list; Forms; Notes document
steps: ## Right after they say yes
Send a welcome message within [one business day] of payment. Thank them, confirm what they bought and list the steps before the first session.
Send your intake form and agreement. Use [your intake form link] and ask for them back within [3 business days].
Send your scheduling link and ask them to book the first session. Include [your booking link] and a date range, such as within the next [10] days.
Add them to your CRM and mark the stage 'Onboarding'. Record the start date, offer, payment status and which forms are outstanding.
## Prepare for the first session
Check that the intake form and signed agreement are back [2 days] before the session. If not, send a friendly reminder with the links again.
Read their answers and your sales call notes. Write down three things you want to understand better.
Create their client folder and notes document. Use your [folder template] so every client is set up the same way.
Prepare your session plan. Decide the goals, your key questions and the agenda for the first [60] minutes.
Send a reminder [24 hours] before the session. Include the time, how to join and anything they should bring.
## Run the first session and follow up
Open the session by confirming their goals and what success looks like in [30 or 90] days. Write down their own words.
Agree on one or two actions they will take before the next session. Put a date on each.
Send a recap within [24 hours] of the session. Include what you agreed, their actions and the date of the next session.
Book the next session before you end the call, or send the link the same day.
Update your CRM stage to 'Active client'. Done means the client has had their first session and knows exactly what comes next.

title: Send the welcome package
purpose: A clear welcome package tells new clients what to expect and what to do first, so they feel confident from day one. Done means the client has everything they need, knows their first action and the send is logged.
tools: Email; Document or PDF tool; Forms; CRM or contact list
steps: ## Assemble the package

Decide what goes in the package. Typical items are a welcome note, a what to expect guide, your contact details, your scheduling link, forms and one starter resource. Keep it to what they need in the first week.
Write a short personal welcome note. Mention something they told you in your sales conversation and keep it under [150 words].
Write a one-page 'what to expect' guide. Cover the timeline, session format, response times, and how to book or reschedule.
List your contact details and working hours. Include [your email], [your phone number] and [your usual response time].
Gather the forms and resources. Include the intake form, agreement, payment receipt and [one helpful starter resource].
## Send the package
Check every link and attachment. Open them in a private browser window so you see what the client sees.
Send it within [one business day] of payment. Use a clear subject line such as 'Welcome to [your business name]: your next steps'.
Put the most important action first. For example, 'Book your first session here'. Keep the list to no more than [3] actions.
Mail any physical items right away if they are part of your offer. Send the client the tracking number or delivery date.
## Confirm and record
Log the send in your CRM. Record the date, what was included and who sent it.
Check for a reply or completed forms after [two business days]. If nothing has arrived, send a short, friendly nudge.
Note anything the client found unclear and update your package. Small fixes after each new client make the next welcome better.
Confirm the client has everything and knows their next step. Done means no one needs to ask 'what happens now?'

title: Run a client kickoff call
purpose: The kickoff call aligns you and your client on goals, how you will work together and the first steps. Done means both of you leave with the same understanding, written actions with dates, and a next session booked.
tools: Calendar; Video call or phone; Notes document; CRM or contact list
steps: ## Before the call
Confirm the time and send the link or number [24 hours] ahead. Add a three-line agenda so they know what to expect.
Review their intake form, agreement and sales call notes. Keep them open in front of you during the call.
Plan an agenda for [45 to 60] minutes. Cover introductions, goals, how you will work together, first steps and questions.
Open a fresh notes document for the call. If you plan to record, make a note to ask for permission at the start.
## During the call
Open with a warm welcome and the agenda. Say how long you have and what you hope they leave with.
Ask what they most want from working with you. Listen, and write down their exact words.
Define success together. Ask 'What would make this feel worthwhile in [30, 60 or 90] days?' and write down one to three outcomes.
Explain how you will work together. Cover session schedule, how to reach you, your response times and what you need from them.
Agree on the first steps. Write each action with an owner and a due date.
Ask about obstacles. For example: 'What might get in the way over the next two weeks?' Agree how you will handle them.
Leave time for questions. Finish by asking 'What else would help you feel confident?'
## After the call
Send a recap within [24 hours]. Include their goals, the agreed actions with dates and the next session date.
Save your notes, the success measures and key dates to the client folder and your CRM.
Set a calendar reminder for your next check-in. Done means the client has a written plan and you both know what happens next.

title: Collect client intake information and signed agreements
purpose: You need the right information and a signed agreement before real work begins. This process collects both quickly and securely, and ends with complete records and a client who knows what happens next.
tools: Forms; Agreement or e-signature tool; Email; Secure file storage; CRM or contact list
steps: ## Prepare your documents
List the questions you truly need answered. Keep only those that change how you serve the client, such as contact details, goals, history, preferences and [anything specific to your service].
Keep sensitive questions to a minimum and explain why you ask. Check with your [attorney or licensed professional] about privacy rules that apply to your work.
Build the intake form in [your form tool]. Test it by filling it in yourself on both your phone and your computer.
Review your agreement template. Confirm it covers scope, fees, payment terms, cancellation, confidentiality and how either side can end it. Have your [attorney] review it.
## Send and collect
Send the form and agreement together in one message. Say how long it takes, such as [10 minutes], and give a due date of [3 business days].
Tell them what happens with their information. Use one sentence on where it is stored and who can see it.
Send a reminder on day [2]. Keep it friendly and include both links again.
Offer another way if they struggle. For example, a short phone call where you fill it in together, or a PDF version.
Check each submission when it arrives. Look for blank required fields, unclear answers, and a signed and dated agreement.
## File and confirm
Save copies in the client folder in [your secure storage]. Name them clearly, such as [Client name - Intake - date], and limit who can open them.
Add key details to your CRM, such as contact information, goals and the agreement date.
Send a confirmation. Thank them, tell them what you received and say what comes next.
Set a reminder to review the agreement on [renewal or review date]. Done means both documents are complete, filed and confirmed.

title: Set up a new client in your systems
purpose: Setting up each client the same way prevents missed invoices, lost files and double-booked sessions. Done means the client's record, billing, calendar and files are all in place before the first session.
tools: CRM or contact list; Invoicing tool; Calendar; File storage; Email
steps: ## Record the client
Create or update the contact in your CRM or contact list. Enter full name, email, phone, [how they found you] and tag them as 'Client'.
Record the offer and key dates. Include package name, price, start date, end or renewal date and payment terms.
Attach the signed agreement and intake form to the record, or add links to where they are saved.
## Set up billing and scheduling
Set up the invoice or recurring payment in [your invoicing tool]. Match the amount and schedule in the agreement, then preview it before it goes out.
Confirm the payment method or payment link works. Send a test or check the status yourself.
Create the recurring calendar events. Set the right length, add the video link and turn on reminders.
Add your rescheduling and cancellation rules to the calendar invite or booking page, using [your policy].
## Set up working files
Create the client folder with standard subfolders, such as [Agreements, Notes, Deliverables, Billing]. Use the naming style [Client name - Year].
Set sharing permissions. Share only what the client needs, and check that no other client's files are visible.
Create the client notes document from your [notes template]. Paste in the goals and key dates.
Add them to your email lists only for what they agreed to. Include the newsletter only if they opted in.
Set reminders for key dates, such as the first check-in, renewal and final session.
Open the record once more and check each item above. Done means you could hand this client to someone else and they would find everything.

title: Run the first 30 days check-in plan
purpose: The first month decides whether a client feels supported or forgotten. This plan schedules four short check-ins so problems surface early, wins are noticed and the client reaches day 30 with momentum.
tools: Calendar; Email; Phone or video call; CRM or contact list; Notes document
steps: ## Plan the check-ins
Add four check-ins to your calendar when the client starts. Use days [3], [7], [14] and [30], and attach a task in your CRM for each.
Decide the format for each one. For example: a short message on day 3, a message on day 7, a [15-minute] call on day 14 and a longer review on day 30.
Prepare a short list of questions to reuse. Include 'What is going well?', 'What is unclear?' and 'What would help most this week?'
## Run the check-ins
Send a day 3 message. Ask if they have everything they need and whether anything is unclear. Reply to any answer the same day.
Send a day 7 message. Ask how the first action went and offer one tip to help with the next.
Hold a day 14 call or send a voice note. Review progress against the goals you agreed at kickoff and adjust the plan if needed.
Hold a day 30 review. Compare results with their goals, point out specific wins and agree on priorities for the next [30] days.
Log each check-in in your CRM right after it happens. Record how they are feeling, what they said and what you will do.
Act on any concern within [one business day]. A quick, caring response matters more than a perfect one.
## Close the first month
Ask for feedback at day 30. Use [2 or 3] questions, such as 'What has been most useful?' and 'What should I do differently?'
Ask for a testimonial or referral only if they are clearly happy. Make it easy with [your testimonial form or referral link].
Agree on the next stretch together. Confirm sessions, goals and any change to the plan, and send a short written summary.
Check that all four check-ins were done and logged. Done means the client knows you are paying attention and what comes next.

title: Answer client emails and messages the same day
purpose: Clients should never wonder whether you received their message. This process keeps every email and message answered, or at least acknowledged, within [one business day], with nothing left unread at the end of each working day.
tools: Email; Messaging apps; CRM or contact list; Calendar
steps: ## Set up your inbox

List every place clients can reach you. Write down your [email address], [text or messaging apps], [social media inbox] and [website contact form] on one sheet, then close or stop checking any channel you do not want to support.
Set your response promise. Choose a window such as within one business day, then add it to your email signature and contact page so clients know what to expect.
Turn on an after-hours auto-reply. Write two sentences with the date you will reply by and an [urgent contact option] for true emergencies only.
Create three folders or labels: Needs Reply, Waiting on Client, and Done. Move each message into one of them so your main inbox stays at or near zero.
## Daily rhythm
Block two 20-minute message windows on your calendar. Pick fixed times such as [10:00 am] and [3:30 pm] so replies do not depend on spare moments.
Sort new messages at the start of each window. Label each as Answer now (under five minutes), Needs research, or Not for me, and hand the last group to [team member or vendor] the same day.
Reply to the quick ones first. Start with the answer rather than a long greeting, and end with one clear next step if there is one.
Acknowledge the longer ones today. Send a short note with thanks, what you are looking into, and the date you will reply by, then put that date on your calendar.
Log anything that affects the relationship. Add a note in your [CRM or contact list] when a message contains a request, a concern or a decision.
## End of day check
Empty your Needs Reply folder. Before you close for the day, confirm every message has a reply or an acknowledgment that includes a date.
Nudge stale items in Waiting on Client. Send one short, friendly follow-up to anyone who has been quiet for [three business days].
Review the week on [Friday]. Note which messages were slow and why, then adjust your windows or saved replies. Done looks like: nothing sitting unanswered past your promised window.

title: Handle a client complaint
purpose: A complaint handled well can strengthen a relationship. This process helps you respond calmly, find out what happened, fix it fairly, and learn from it, ending with a client who feels heard and a record of what changed.
tools: Email; Phone or video call; CRM or contact list; Complaint log
steps: ## Receive the complaint
Acknowledge it within [a few hours]. Send a short note saying you have read their message, you take it seriously, and you will follow up by [date].
Pause before you reply in detail. Do not defend yourself or explain in the first response. Read the message twice, and if it feels heated, wait until you are calm.
Offer the channel that suits them. Ask whether they would prefer to talk by phone, video or in writing so they can say everything they need to say.
Start a record. Open a note in your [CRM or contact list] with the date, client name, what happened in their words, and what they say they want.
## Understand and resolve
Listen for the full story before you respond. Then repeat back what you heard in one or two sentences and ask whether you have it right.
Check the facts on your side. Review [emails, invoices, notes and your agreement] to see what was promised and what actually happened. Do not guess.
Own what is yours. If you made a mistake, say so plainly and apologize once, with no excuses. If part of it is a misunderstanding, explain gently using the facts.

Offer a specific remedy from options you decided in advance, such as [redo the work, a credit, a partial refund or an extra session]. Check with your [attorney or accountant] if refunds or contract terms are involved.
Confirm the next step in writing. Send a short summary of what you will do and by when, and ask the client to reply to confirm.
## Follow through and learn
Do exactly what you promised, on the date you promised. Put the date on your calendar and tell the client as soon as it is complete.
Check in a week later. Send a brief message asking whether the matter is fully settled and whether anything else is needed.

Record the cause and one improvement in [your complaint log]. Change a process, template or expectation so it is less likely to happen again. Done looks like: client confirms resolved, record updated, one improvement noted.

title: Handle a refund or cancellation request
purpose: Refund and cancellation requests are easier when you follow the same fair steps every time. This process keeps the client treated with respect, your policy applied consistently, and your records complete from request to confirmation.
tools: Email; Invoicing or payment tool; CRM or contact list; Spreadsheet log
steps: ## Before a request arrives
Write your policy in plain language. State what is refundable, the deadlines, and how cancellations work, based on [your agreement]. Have your [attorney] review it once.
Put the policy where clients will see it. Include it in [your agreement], [your website page] and [your booking or payment confirmation].
Create a refund and cancellation log. Use a spreadsheet or your CRM with columns for date, client, offer, amount, reason, decision and date completed.
## When a request comes in
Reply within [one business day]. Thank them, confirm you received the request, and say when they will hear your decision.
Pull their agreement and payment record. Check what they signed, what they paid, what has been delivered, and where they are in the term.
Ask one gentle question if the reason is unclear. Understanding why helps you improve, but never make an answer a condition of the request.
Decide using your policy. Approve, partially approve or decline. If an exception makes sense for the relationship, approve it and mark it as an exception in the log.
Write the decision kindly and clearly. State the outcome, the amount, the timing, and what happens to any remaining sessions or access, without a long justification.
## Complete and close out
Process the change in your [payment processor or invoicing tool]. Stop recurring charges, cancel future appointments, and remove access to [portal or materials] on the agreed date.
Send a confirmation with the amount and when to expect it. Mention that banks can take [5 to 10 business days] to post a refund.
Update your records. Change the client status in your [CRM or contact list], remove them from active email series, and complete the log. Ask your [accountant] how to record refunds.

Leave the door open. Send a short thank-you note with an invitation to return in future, and one optional question on how you could have served them better. Done looks like: confirmed, funds moved, records updated.

title: Resolve a technical problem for a client
purpose: When something breaks for a client, they want it fixed and a clear voice guiding them. This process helps you gather the right details, work through fixes in order, and confirm the problem is solved and documented.
tools: Email; Screen recording or screenshot tool; Support log or CRM; Video call
steps: ## Capture the problem
Acknowledge it right away. Tell the client you have it, you are working on it, and when they will hear from you next.
Ask for exactly what you need. Request what they were trying to do, what happened instead, the device and browser or app they used, and a screenshot or short screen recording.
Ask when it started and whether it ever worked. Note anything that changed recently, such as an update, a new device or a new password.
Log it in [your support list or CRM] with the date, client, description, and a priority of Blocked (cannot continue) or Inconvenient.
## Diagnose and fix
Try to reproduce it yourself using the same steps. If you cannot, tell the client and ask for one more detail rather than guessing.
Try the simple fixes first. Refresh, restart, sign out and back in, use another browser, clear the cache, check their connection, and confirm [their account or payment status].
Check your own side. Look at [your platform status page], recent changes you made, expired links, permissions and settings.
Give one instruction at a time. Use numbered steps, short sentences and screenshots, and avoid sending a long list of possible options.
Escalate after [30 minutes] or if it is outside your control. Contact [software provider support] with the description and screenshots, and tell the client you have done so.
Offer a workaround so they are not stuck. For example, send the file by email or move the session to a phone call while the fix is in progress.
## Confirm and prevent
Ask the client to try again and tell you the result. Do not mark it resolved until they confirm it works.
Update your log with the cause, the fix, and how long it took.

Prevent a repeat. If this could happen to other clients, add a note to your [help library or FAQ] or adjust your onboarding. Done looks like: client confirms it works, log closed, help article added if useful.

title: Keep your help library and FAQ current
purpose: A current help library answers common questions before clients have to ask, and saves you repeat typing. This process builds the list of questions, writes clear answers, and reviews them on a schedule so nothing goes stale.
tools: Shared document or help page; Email; CRM or contact list; Calendar
steps: ## Collect what clients ask
Choose where your library lives. Pick one place, such as [a help page, shared document or folder], where clients can find it, and add the link to your email signature and welcome messages.
Start a running question list. Whenever a client asks something, add the question to [your question list] with the date and how often it comes up.
Mine your sources once a month. Skim your sent emails, messages, call notes and support log for questions you have answered more than once.
## Write and organize
Pick the top ten questions first. Rank them by how often they come up or how much of your time they take.
Write each answer in plain language. Use the question as the title, then give the answer in two to five short sentences or numbered steps, with a link or screenshot if it helps.
Use your clients' own words. Title each entry with the phrase they actually use, not your internal term.
Group entries into a few categories such as [Getting started, Scheduling, Payments, Technical help and Programs] so clients can scan quickly.
End every entry with a way to reach you, such as [your support email], and add a last-reviewed date at the top.
## Keep it current
Update the library the same day anything changes. When you change a price, policy, tool or schedule, search the library for the old information and correct it.
Block [one hour] each [quarter] to review. Open every entry, check the links, and remove or rewrite anything outdated.
Use the library in your replies. When a question is already answered, send the link with one personal sentence and ask whether it helped.

Look at what is missing. Note which entries clients use and which questions still arrive by email. Done looks like: top questions answered, every entry reviewed within the last [90 days], and the link shared with clients.

title: Run a client satisfaction check
purpose: Regular check-ins show you how clients really feel before small problems grow. This process asks a few simple questions at set moments, follows up personally, and turns the answers into one improvement at a time.
tools: Online form or email; CRM or contact list; Calendar; Spreadsheet
steps: ## Plan the check
Decide when to ask. Choose natural moments such as [after the first month, at the midpoint and at the end of the program] and add them to your calendar as reminders.
Pick one format. Use a short online form, a brief email or a five-minute call, and keep the whole thing to five minutes or less.
Write three to five questions. Include an overall rating from 1 to 10, what is working best, what could be better, whether they would recommend you, and [one question specific to your service].
Build the form or template once at [your form link] and save it so each check takes you two minutes to send.
## Send and collect
Send it personally. Use the client's name and add one sentence on why you are asking and that honest answers help you serve them better.
Send one friendly reminder after [three days] if there is no reply, and then stop. Offer a quick call for anyone who prefers to talk.
Record each answer. Add the date, score and comments to the client's record in your [CRM or contact list].
## Act on the answers
Thank every client within [two business days] and name one thing you will do or have already done because of their feedback.
Reach out personally to low scores. Any rating of [6 or below], or any concern, gets a personal call or message from you within [one business day].
Invite happy clients to the next step. Once they say they are pleased, ask for [a testimonial, a review at your review link, or a referral].
Review the results each [quarter]. Look at the average score, common praise and common concerns, then choose one improvement and add it to your task list.
Close the loop. Done looks like: every client asked at the planned moment, every reply answered, and one improvement chosen and scheduled.

title: Schedule and confirm client appointments
purpose: Clear scheduling means clients show up on time, prepared, and at the right place. This process sets up your availability, confirms and reminds every booking, and handles changes and no-shows the same way each time.
tools: Calendar; Booking link; Email or text; CRM or contact list
steps: ## Set up your scheduling
Define your available hours. Choose the days and times you take appointments, a buffer between them, and a maximum number per day of [number]. Block your personal time first.
Create one appointment type for each service in your calendar or booking tool. Include the name, length, location or video link, and any preparation needed.
Publish your booking link. Put [your booking link] in your email signature, your website and your welcome messages so clients book without back and forth.
Write your confirmation message once. Include the date, time, time zone, location or link, how to reschedule, and your cancellation terms: [your policy].
## Book and confirm
Confirm every booking within [one business day] if it is not sent automatically. Make sure it is on your calendar with the client's name and contact details.
State the time zone in every invite and message. If the client is in another region, double-check the converted time, especially around clock changes.
Send preparation details by [two days before]. Include what to bring, any forms to complete, and [the questions you want them to think about].
Send reminders at [48 hours] and [two hours] before. Include the link or address and a simple way to reschedule.
Handle changes in writing. Offer two or three alternate times, update your calendar, send a new confirmation straight away, and delete the old slot.
## After the appointment
Mark the outcome in your [CRM or contact list] as attended, rescheduled or missed, so your records stay accurate.
Follow up with missed appointments the same day. Send a kind note offering to rebook, and mention your policy only if it applies.
Book the next appointment before you end each one, or send the booking link within [24 hours].
Check next week's calendar every [Friday]. Done looks like: every appointment confirmed, preparation sent, and no double bookings.

title: Send a weekly client update
purpose: A short, predictable weekly update builds trust and cuts down on check-in questions. This process gathers what happened, writes it simply, and sends it at the same time every week so clients always know where things stand.
tools: Email; Task list or project notes; Calendar; CRM or contact list
steps: ## Gather
Pick a fixed day and time. Choose [Friday at 2:00 pm], and add a recurring 30-minute block to your calendar so the update does not slip.
Decide who receives it. List [active clients or the clients on each project], and decide whether you will send one shared version or a personalized one.
Collect the facts from [your task list, project notes and calendar]. Write down what was finished, what is in progress, what comes next, and what you need from the client.
## Write
Open with a one-sentence headline. State the single most important thing, such as that the draft is ready for review or the work is on track.
List what was completed. Use two to four short bullets in plain language that show results rather than activity.
List what is next. Give two or three items, each with a date.
State what you need from the client. Be specific and give a date. If you need nothing, say so, because that is useful to know.
Flag any delay or risk honestly. Say what happened, the new date, and what you are doing about it, and do not bury it at the bottom.
Close with an invitation to reply and your name. Keep the whole update under [200 words].
## Send and follow up
Proofread before sending. Check names, dates and links, and read it aloud once to catch awkward lines.
Send it from [your email address] at the planned time. Use a scheduled send if you finish early.
Save a copy in the client's record in your [CRM or project folder], so you have a running history.
Answer replies within [one business day]. Done looks like: every client received the update on schedule, replies answered, and a copy saved.

title: Send a monthly progress report to clients
purpose: A monthly report shows clients the value they are getting and keeps goals in view. This process collects the same data each month, presents it clearly and honestly, and turns it into agreed priorities for the next month.
tools: Document or spreadsheet; Email; Calendar; CRM or contact list
steps: ## Prepare
Set the report date. Choose [the first Monday of each month], add a [60-minute] block to your calendar, and set a reminder three days before.
Pull the same data each month from [attendance records, goals, completed tasks and key metrics], so reports are comparable.
Compare to last month and to the original goals in the client's [plan or agreement], and note where they have moved forward, stayed level or slipped.
Choose the top three wins. Include a number or a specific example for each wherever you can.
## Write
Use one consistent layout. Set headings for Summary, Wins, Numbers, Challenges, Next month's focus, and What I need from you.
Write the summary in three or four plain sentences. Say where they started, where they are now, and what that means for them.
Show the numbers simply. Use a small table or short list with last month's figure beside this month's, and explain any change in one line.
Be honest about challenges. Say what has not moved, the likely reason, and what you suggest. For tax, legal or medical points, point them to their own [accountant, attorney or licensed professional].
Set next month's focus. Choose no more than three priorities, each with an owner and a date.
## Deliver and follow up
Send the report by [date]. Attach a PDF or share a link, and offer a [20-minute] call to go through it together.
Hold the review call if booked. Start with wins, then challenges, then agree on priorities and take notes.
Save the report in the client's file and record the agreed priorities in your [CRM or task list].
Check in at the midpoint of the month with a short message. Done looks like: report sent on time, priorities agreed, and a midpoint check scheduled.

title: Run the weekly team meeting
purpose: A short, consistent weekly meeting keeps everyone aligned on priorities and removes blockers early. This process sets the agenda, keeps the meeting tight, and ends with clear actions that have an owner and a date.
tools: Calendar; Video call or meeting room; Shared document; Task list
steps: ## Before the meeting
Set a fixed time. Choose [Monday at 9:30 am] for [30 minutes], and send a recurring invite with [your video link or room].
Create one shared agenda document at [shared document link]. Ask everyone to add their items by [the day before].
Use the same agenda each week. Cover wins, priorities for the week, blockers, decisions needed, and action items, and write a time limit next to each.
Prepare for ten minutes beforehand. Review last week's action items, your calendar for the week ahead, and any key numbers.
## During the meeting
Start on time. Begin within a minute of the start time even if someone is missing, so people learn to arrive on time.
Begin with wins. Ask each person to share one win from last week in about a minute.
Review last week's actions. For each one, mark it done, not done or moved, and do not re-discuss it, just update the status.
Go around for this week's priorities. Each person states their top three in a sentence or two.
Raise blockers and decisions. Limit each to [five minutes], and if it is not settled, assign an owner and a date and take it offline.
Close by reading back every action item. State what, who and by when, and add each one to [your task list] before the meeting ends.
## After the meeting
Send notes within [two hours]. List decisions and action items with owner and date, in [your shared channel or email].
Check progress midweek. Glance at [your task list] and message anyone who looks stuck.
Review the meeting each month. Ask the team what is useful and what to cut. Done looks like: the meeting ends on time, every action has an owner and a date, and notes go out the same day.

title: Handle a no-show or late client
purpose: Give every late arrival or missed appointment the same calm, fair response, so you protect your time and keep the relationship. Done means the client has been contacted once, the record is updated and a new time is booked or offered.
tools: Calendar; Phone or text; Email; CRM or contact list; Invoicing tool
steps: ## When the client is late
Wait [10 minutes] before you decide anything. Use the time to check your messages and email in case they wrote to say they are delayed.

Send one short check-in message. Try: 'Hi [client name], I am here and ready for our [time] session. Are you on your way?' Send it at the [5 minute] mark, by text or email, whichever they answer fastest.

Decide what is possible if they arrive. If they show up within [15 minutes], offer a shortened session that ends at the original time so you do not run into your next commitment. Tell them the plan before you begin.
## When the client does not show
Make one more attempt to reach them. Call once or send a second message at [15 minutes] past the start. Do not send a long string of messages.
Release the slot. Mark the appointment as a no-show in your calendar and use the time for other work. Do not keep waiting past what your policy says.
Record it in your CRM or contact list. Add a dated note with the scheduled time, what you sent and whether they replied. Stick to plain facts so the record is easy to review later.

Check your [late and no-show policy]. Decide whether a fee, a lost session or nothing applies. If it is a first miss or there was a real emergency, you can choose to waive it once and note that you did.
## Follow up and prevent a repeat
Send a follow-up within one business day. Say you missed them, state the policy in one sentence and offer two new times with [your booking link]. Keep the tone kind and free of blame.
Send any fee in writing. If a fee applies, send the invoice from [your invoicing tool] with a short note. Ask your [accountant] how to record it if you are unsure.
Look for a pattern. If this is the second miss within [60 days], ask what is getting in the way. Offer a different time of day, a reminder text or a shorter session.
Check your reminders. Confirm automatic reminders go out [24 hours] and [2 hours] before each session, and that your confirmation message includes your policy.
## Closing checks
Confirm the loop is closed. The slot is marked, the client has been contacted, a new time is booked or offered, any fee is handled and the note is saved in their record.

title: Announce a launch or a change to clients
purpose: Tell the right people about something new or different clearly and early, so no one is surprised. Done means every affected client has the message, your public pages match and questions are answered.
tools: Email; CRM or contact list; Website; Social media; Calendar
steps: ## Get clear before you write
Write the change in one sentence. Complete this: 'Starting [date], [what is changing].' If you cannot say it in one sentence, the message will confuse people.
List who is affected. Filter your CRM or contact list for [current clients], [past clients] and [waitlist]. Decide who needs full details and who only needs a short mention.
Answer the three questions people will ask. What is different for me, what do I need to do, and what will it cost me? Write a short answer to each and add the date by which they must act.
Check what you have already promised. Review agreements, packages and prices you have committed to. If the change touches money or terms, confirm the wording with your [attorney or accountant] first.
## Write and schedule the message
Draft the main message in your email tool. Put the news in the first two lines, the reason in one or two sentences, then the action and the date. Aim for under [250] words.
Give one clear next step. Use a single link or instruction such as [your booking link] or 'reply to this email'. Several choices lower the number of replies.
Send a test to yourself. Check links, names, dates and how it looks on a phone. Ask [a trusted colleague] to read it once if you can.
Pick the send time. Choose [a weekday morning] when people are most likely to read it. Avoid sending right before a day you are unavailable.
Post a shorter version where clients look for you. Share a brief note on [your website or social channel] that points back to the full message.
## Support and follow up
Prepare short replies for likely questions. Write three or four standard answers so you can respond within [one business day].
Remind those who have not acted. After [5 days], filter for people who have not taken the next step and send a short reminder with the same link.
Update every page that mentions it. Change prices, descriptions and policies on [your website], booking page, proposals and email signature so nothing contradicts the news.
## Closing checks
Confirm everything is complete. All affected people have the message, public pages match, replies are answered and you have saved the wording and date in [your CRM or notes].

title: Prepare for and run a client session
purpose: Make every session focused, on time and useful, so the client leaves with clear actions and you leave with a record. Done means the session started and ended on time, actions are agreed and quick notes are saved.
tools: Calendar; Video meeting tool; CRM or client notes; Email
steps: ## Before the session
Read the client's file. Open [your CRM or client notes] and review the last session, open actions and their stated goal. About 10 minutes is enough.
Write a three-line plan. List the main goal for today, one or two topics to cover and the outcome you want them to leave with.
Confirm the session. Send a short message at least [24 hours] ahead with the time, [video link or address] and anything they should prepare.
Set up your materials. Open the documents or tools you will use, and test your audio, camera or room [15 minutes] before the start.
Clear your space. Close email and messages, silence your phone and have water and a pen ready so you can give your full attention.
## During the session
Start on time with a short check-in. Greet them, confirm how much time you have and ask what they most want from today. Two minutes is enough.
Review progress since last time. Ask what they completed and what got in the way. Name the wins first, then the obstacles, without judgment.
Go through your planned topics one at a time. If something new comes up, note it in a 'parking lot' and return to it at the end if time allows.
Agree on next actions before you stop. Say the one to three actions out loud with a due date for each, and ask them to repeat them back in their own words.
## Close the session
End on time. Begin wrapping up [5 minutes] before the end, summarize, confirm the next date using [your booking link] and thank them.
Jot down raw notes straight away. Capture actions, key phrases and anything you promised while it is fresh. Full notes can be written afterward.
Take a short reset before the next thing. Stand up, drink water and clear your notes window so the next person gets your full attention.
Check that the session is complete. It started and ended on time, the client has actions with dates, the next session is set and your quick notes are in their file.

title: After each session: notes and next steps
purpose: Turn every session into a clear record and a follow-up the client can act on. Done means notes are saved, the recap is sent, your own tasks are created and the next session is booked.
tools: CRM or client notes; Email; Task list; Calendar; Invoicing tool
steps: ## Write up the session
Block time right after the session. Set aside [15 minutes] on the same day while details are fresh. Waiting past 24 hours makes them fade.
Use the same note format every time. Use headings such as what we covered, key insights, decisions and actions agreed. Consistent notes are easier to find later.
Record each action with an owner and a date. Write who does what by when, including anything you promised to send or do.

Keep private notes separate from shared notes. Put your own observations in a [private section] and share only what the client should see. Check record-keeping rules for your field with your [licensed professional or attorney].
## Send the follow-up
Send a recap within [one business day]. Include the agreed actions, dates and any resources you promised. Keep it short enough to read on one screen.
Attach or link what you promised. Add worksheets, recordings or tools directly so the client does not have to ask.
Remind them of the next session. Include the date and time, or [your booking link] if it is not yet booked.
## Update your records
Update the client's status. Change the stage or tag in [your CRM], note sessions used and remaining in their package, and set the next follow-up date.
Create tasks for your own actions. Add each promise to [your task list] with a due date so nothing slips.
Flag anything for billing. If the session is billable or the package is nearly used, mark it for invoicing in [your invoicing tool].
Set a mid-point reminder. If it suits your style, schedule a brief check-in between sessions, such as a two-line message [3 to 4 days] after.
## Closing checks
Confirm the follow-up is complete. Notes are saved, the recap is sent, tasks are created, the next session is booked and the client record is current.

title: Deliver a project or package from start to finish
purpose: Run each project or package the same way, from agreed scope to final handover, so the client always knows where things stand. Done means the work is approved, delivered, invoiced and reviewed.
tools: Project board or task list; Email; Shared folder; Invoicing tool; CRM or contact list
steps: ## Set up the work
Confirm the scope in writing. Re-read the signed [proposal or agreement] and list what is included, what is not and the delivery date. Send a short summary to the client for a quick yes.
Break the work into milestones. Divide it into [3 to 5] stages, each with a clear outcome and a date. Note what you need from the client at each stage.
Set up a project record. Create a folder or board in [your project tool] with milestones, due dates and links. Share the parts the client needs to see.
Collect what you need up front. Send a checklist of information, files and approvals with a return date. Late client inputs are the most common cause of delays.
## Deliver in stages
Update progress each week. Mark what is done, in progress and at risk in [your project tool], so you can see problems early.
Send the client a short update every [week]. Use three lines: done, in progress and what you need from them.
Present each milestone for approval. Send the work with a clear request such as 'please reply by [date] with approval or one combined list of changes'.
Handle change requests in writing. If a request falls outside scope, say so kindly, give the cost and time impact and get a yes before you proceed.
## Finish and hand over
Check the final work against the scope list. Go line by line through what was promised and fix any gaps before you deliver.
Deliver everything in one organized place. Share a folder or link with clearly named files and a short note on what each one is and how to use it.
Confirm acceptance and invoice. Ask the client to confirm the work is complete, record the date and send the final invoice from [your invoicing tool] as agreed.
## Closing checks
Hold a short review. Note what went well, what took longer than planned and one change for next time. Save it in [your notes].
Confirm the project is closed. Every milestone is approved, files are delivered, the final invoice is sent and the client record is updated.

title: Quality check before you deliver
purpose: Catch mistakes and gaps before the client does, with the same short checklist every time. Done means the work matches the brief, the details are clean and a second person has looked at it.
tools: Checklist or task list; Shared folder; Email
steps: ## Check the content
Reopen the original request. Read the signed scope or the client's brief before you look at your work. Write down the three things they care about most.
Compare the work to the brief line by line. Tick each promised item and mark anything missing, extra or changed from what was agreed.
Test it against the client's real goal. Ask whether they could use this tomorrow without asking a question. If not, add what is missing.
Verify numbers and facts. Check figures, dates, names, prices and quotes against your source. Redo any calculation a second way.
## Check the details
Proofread out loud. Read the text aloud or use a read-aloud feature, since your ear catches what your eyes skip. Double-check the client's name and business name.
Test every link, form and file. Click each link and open each attachment, ideally on a second device, and confirm files are named clearly.
Check formatting and branding. Confirm fonts, colors, logos and layout match [your brand guide] or the client's. View it on both a phone and a computer.
Check privacy. Remove hidden comments, tracked changes, other clients' details and internal pricing. Look at file properties before you share.
## Get a second view and sign off
Ask someone else to review it. Give [a colleague or trusted peer] the brief and [15 minutes] to read it cold. Ask what is unclear.
Fix and re-check. After changes, repeat the checks the edits could have affected. A quick edit is not automatically safe.
Leave it for a short while if you can. If the deadline allows, step away for [an hour] and give it one last look.
Sign off in writing. Note the date, who checked it and that it passed on your checklist. Only then send it to the client.
Confirm the check is complete. The checklist is finished, errors are fixed and the final file is named and stored in [your shared folder].

title: Run a group program or cohort week
purpose: Run each week of a group program the same way, so participants feel looked after and you are never scrambling. Done means the live session ran, the recap is out, quiet participants are contacted and next week is adjusted.
tools: Video meeting tool; Email; Community space or group chat; CRM or tracker; Calendar
steps: ## Before the week
Review the week's plan. Open your [program outline] and confirm the topic, the outcome for participants and the materials needed.
Send a preview message [2 days] before. Include the date, time, link, topic and one thing to prepare. Put the link in the same message as the time.
Check where each person is. Review attendance, completed work and messages in [your tracker or community space]. Note anyone who seems stuck or quiet.
Prepare your session. Plan [2 or 3] teaching points, one exercise and one discussion question. Test the video tool and screen share [15 minutes] early.
## During the live session

Start on time with a short welcome. Greet people by name, restate confidentiality and how to take part, and say if the session is recorded. Check your local rules on consent with your [attorney] if unsure.
Open with wins and check-ins. Invite [one minute] each or use the chat. This builds community and shows you where people are.
Teach in short blocks. Teach for [10 to 15 minutes], then give people something to do, answer or discuss.
Use breakout or pair work. Give a clear prompt, a time limit and a way to report back. Visit each group briefly.
End with one commitment each. Ask everyone to say or type what they will do before next time, and confirm the next date.
## After the session and between weeks
Send the recap within [24 hours]. Include the recording link, slides, the exercise and the commitment list, and highlight the one thing to do first.
Reach out to anyone who missed or struggled. Send a personal message and offer a short catch-up or a summary. Contact anyone quiet for more than [one week].
Log attendance and notes. Update [your tracker or CRM] with attendance, completed work and observations to shape next week.
## Closing checks
Confirm the week is complete. The recap is sent, the recording is shared, missed participants are contacted, the tracker is updated and next week's plan is adjusted.

title: Wrap up an engagement and offboard a client
purpose: End every client engagement cleanly, so the client has what they need, the money and records are settled and the door stays open. Done means files are handed over, final invoice is paid or sent, feedback is requested and the record is archived.
tools: Email; CRM or contact list; Shared folder; Invoicing tool; Calendar
