steps: ## Prepare for the ending
Confirm the end date. Check your agreement for the end date or remaining sessions and tell the client at least [two weeks] ahead so there are no surprises.
Review what was achieved. Re-read the original goals and your session notes. List results, clear wins and what remains.
Decide what comes next. Choose whether to offer a continuation, a maintenance option, a referral to someone else or nothing, and prepare it with [your price].
## Final session and handover
Hold a final review. Go through results with the client and ask what changed for them and what they want to keep doing. Take notes.
Hand over everything that belongs to them. Send files, documents, recordings and templates in one organized folder. Remove your access to their accounts and ask them to change any shared passwords.
Write a one-page 'what happens next' summary. Include results, steps they can take on their own and how to reach you, if they can.
Settle the final invoice. Check that all invoices are paid and send any last one from [your invoicing tool]. Ask your [accountant] about any refund or credit question.
Mention the next step once. Share your continuation option or referral ask lightly, with no pressure, and leave the decision with them.
## Close the account
Ask for feedback. Send [two or three] simple questions with one link, and ask permission before you share their words publicly.
Ask for referrals. If they were happy, ask who they know that could use your help and offer [a referral link or short blurb].
Archive their records. Move them to 'past clients' in [your CRM], keep documents for the length your [accountant or attorney] advises and stop active reminders.
Send a closing thank-you. Write a short personal note with the date you finished and an open door. Set a reminder to check in after [3 months].
Confirm offboarding is complete. Files are handed over, access is removed, the invoice is settled, feedback is requested and the record is archived.

title: Plan the week
purpose: Spend [30 minutes] once a week deciding what matters, so the days are driven by priorities and not by whatever arrives first. Done means your calendar has blocked priorities and you know your first task on Monday.
tools: Calendar; Task list; CRM or contact list; Invoicing tool
steps: ## Look back
Set aside [30 minutes] at the same time each week. Pick [Friday afternoon or Sunday evening] and put it on your calendar as a recurring block.
Review last week's list. Mark what got done and what rolled over, and why. Notice patterns, such as tasks that always slip.
Check your numbers. Glance at [inquiries, sales, hours worked and money received] in your CRM and invoicing tool. Write down one thing you notice.
Clear your inbox and loose notes. Turn notes and messages into tasks or delete them, so the plan starts from a clean slate.
## Look ahead
List your fixed commitments first. Open your calendar for next week and mark client sessions, meetings, deadlines and personal commitments.
Choose [three] priorities. Pick the three outcomes that would make the week a success, for example one that brings in revenue, one that serves clients and one that builds your business.
Note what is coming due. Check invoices to send, renewals, follow-ups and deadlines in the next [two weeks].
## Build the plan
Block time for each priority. Put each on the calendar for [60 to 90 minutes] during your best hours of the day. Plan fewer hours than you have.
Leave a buffer. Keep about [20 percent] of the week open for the unexpected, admin and rest.
Batch the small things. Group email, invoicing and bookkeeping into one or two set blocks.
Share the plan if you have a team. Send [your team] a short message with the priorities and who needs what from whom.
Confirm the plan is ready. Your calendar shows blocked priorities, your task list is short and you know exactly what you will start with on Monday.

title: Start-of-day routine
purpose: Begin each work day the same way, so you start with clarity and not with whatever lands in your inbox. Done means your calendar is reviewed, your top three tasks are written down and your first focused block has begun.
tools: Calendar; Task list; Email; Phone or messages
steps: ## Get ready
Start at the same time each day. Begin work at [your start time] so you and your clients know when you are available.
Prepare your space. Clear your desk, open only the tools you need and have water or your usual drink ready.
Take two minutes to settle. Breathe, stretch or note how you feel and how much energy you have. Adjust the day if you are running low.
## Plan the day
Open your calendar. Look at today's sessions, meetings and deadlines. Note the first fixed commitment and what you need to prepare for it.
Scan for urgent messages only. Check [email and messages] for anything time-sensitive or from clients. Reply to urgent items and leave the rest for your set time.
Pick your top [three] tasks. Choose the three from [your task list] that matter most today and write them at the top of your list.
Put a time beside each one. If the total is more than [5 hours], move one to tomorrow.
Protect your first focus block. Schedule [60 to 90 minutes] for the hardest task before you open anything else.
## Review and begin
Prepare for today's sessions. Read the notes for each client you will see and note anything to bring or send.
Check money and follow-ups. Glance at new payments, overdue invoices and leads waiting for a reply. Add what is needed to your list.
Set your message windows. Decide when you will check email and messages, such as [11:00 and 15:00], and say so in your auto-reply if it helps.
Start the first task. Silence notifications and begin right away.
Confirm the start is complete. Your calendar is reviewed, three priorities are written down, urgent messages are handled and the first focus block is under way.

title: Month-end bookkeeping and review
purpose: Keeps your books accurate and current so you always know what you earned, spent and owe. Done when every transaction is categorized, each account matches its statement, and you have reviewed a one-page summary for the month.
tools: Accounting tool or spreadsheet; Bank and card statements; Calendar; Cloud storage
steps: ## Gather the month's records
Block time on your calendar. Book [90 minutes] on the [first Friday] of each month so this happens on schedule instead of whenever you remember.
Pull your statements. Download the month's statements for [business checking account], [business credit card] and [payment processor] so you can match them to your books.
Collect your receipts. Put paper and emailed receipts for the month in one folder named [YYYY-MM]. Anything without a receipt goes on a short find-later list.
## Record and reconcile
Categorize every transaction. Step through the month in your [accounting tool or spreadsheet] and assign each one a category. Mark anything unsure as 'ask my [accountant]' rather than guessing.
Match income to invoices. Check that each deposit lines up with a paid invoice and mark the invoice paid. List any money received with no invoice behind it.
Reconcile each account. Compare the ending balance in your books to the statement balance. Chase any difference until it is zero or explained in a written note.
Review recurring charges. Confirm each subscription is recorded and still needed, and cancel anything you no longer use.
Set aside tax and owner pay. Move [amount or percentage your accountant recommends] into your tax savings account and record your owner pay for the month.
## Review the numbers
Run your summary reports. Open your profit and loss report and cash balance for the month and save a PDF copy in [your records folder].
Compare to last month and your target. Note income, your largest expense categories and profit. Write one sentence on anything that moved more than [10 percent].
List what is owed. Write down unpaid client invoices and unpaid bills with due dates, and decide who you will follow up with this week.
## Close the month
Record your next actions. Write down [up to three] decisions or follow-ups from the review and put a date for each on your calendar.

Mark the month closed. Note the date you finished in [your books log] and lock or flag the month so old entries are not changed by accident. Done looks like zero uncategorized items and balances that match.

title: Invoice clients and collect payment
purpose: Gets every client invoiced promptly and paid on time without awkward chasing. Done when the invoice is sent, the payment is received and recorded, and the client has a receipt.
tools: Invoicing tool; Email; CRM or contact list; Calendar
steps: ## Before you invoice
Confirm what is billable. Check your [agreement or proposal] and your session or project notes so the invoice matches exactly what was agreed and delivered.
Check the client's billing details. Confirm the [legal name or business name], the billing email, and any purchase order number the client needs shown on the invoice.
Apply your standard terms. Use [your payment terms, such as due within 14 days], your accepted payment methods and your [late fee policy, if you have one], the same way every time.
## Send the invoice
Create the invoice in your invoicing tool. Use a clear line item such as '[service name], [dates]' with the amount and a unique invoice number. Check with your [accountant] on whether tax applies.
Add a way to pay. Include [your payment link or payment instructions] so the client can pay in one step.
Send it on the delivery date or agreed billing date. Use a short email covering what the invoice is for, the amount, the due date and how to pay.
Log it. Record the invoice in your [CRM or tracking sheet] with the date sent and the due date.
## Follow up
Put reminders on your calendar. Add the due date plus a check-in one day after it.
Send a friendly reminder before the due date if you like. Something short such as 'A quick note that invoice [number] is due on [date]' works well.
Follow up the day after the due date. Reattach the invoice and the payment link, and keep the tone warm and matter-of-fact.
Make a personal contact if still unpaid after [7 days]. Call or send a direct message, ask if anything is in the way, and offer [a payment plan, if you have one].
## Close it out
Record the payment. Mark the invoice paid with the date and method, and match it to the deposit in your bank account.
Send a receipt and a thank you. Done looks like a paid invoice, a receipt in the client's inbox and the client's record updated.

title: Hire and onboard a contractor or team member
purpose: Brings in help in a clear, fair and well-documented way so the person can start contributing quickly. Done when the agreement is signed, paperwork is on file, access works and the first task is delivered.
tools: Email; Video call tool; Document or contract tool; Password manager; Invoicing or payroll tool
steps: ## Define the role and find the person
Write down the work. List the [3 to 5] main tasks, expected hours per week, the result you want and your budget of [rate or range].
Decide how you will engage them. Rules for contractors and employees differ by location, so confirm the right setup with your [attorney or accountant] before you make an offer.
Share the opportunity. Send a short description to [your network, community or job board] and ask applicants to reply with [examples of past work].
Interview with the same questions. Hold a [20 to 30 minute] call with each finalist and ask for [two references] you can contact.
Offer a small paid trial if useful. Give a [sample task] with a clear brief and a deadline, and pay for it at your normal rate.
## Make it official
Put the terms in writing. Cover scope, rate, payment schedule, confidentiality and how either side can end the arrangement. Have your [attorney] review your template once.
Collect the paperwork. Get the signed agreement, [required tax forms] and payment details, and file them in [your private records folder].
Set up payment. Add the person to [your invoicing or payroll tool] and agree on the pay date.
## Onboard and check in
Give access carefully. Create only the accounts and folders they need and share logins through your password manager, never by email.
Hold a [45 minute] kickoff call. Cover your goals, how you communicate, [response time expectations] and who to ask when they are stuck.
Share a one-page guide. Include your key processes, your tone and style, and [links to templates and examples].
Assign a first small task. Give it a clear due date and say what good looks like.
Schedule check-ins. Book a short review on [day 3, day 14 and day 30], and at day 30 decide together whether to continue, adjust or end.

title: Run a quarterly business review
purpose: Gives you a regular, honest look at your numbers, offers and energy so you can steer on purpose. Done when you have a one-page summary, three goals for next quarter, and dates on your calendar.
tools: Accounting tool or spreadsheet; CRM or contact list; Calendar; Notes document
steps: ## Prepare
Protect the time. Block [half a day] in the last week of the quarter with no client calls and no email.
Pull your numbers. Collect revenue, expenses, profit, new clients, lost clients and hours worked from [your accounting tool and CRM] into one page.
Gather feedback. Read client survey replies, testimonials and any complaints from the past [3 months].
Check last quarter's goals. List each goal and mark it done, partly done or not done.
## Review honestly
Compare results to your targets. Note where you are ahead, on track or behind, and write one sentence on why.
Name your top three wins. Write what caused each one so you can repeat it.
Name what drained you. List the clients, tasks or offers that cost more time or energy than they returned.
Review each offer and price. Decide whether to keep it, change it or retire it based on [your minimum profit or hourly value].
## Plan the next quarter
Set [three] goals. Give each one a measurable target and a date.
Break each goal into first steps. Put the actions for the first [30 days] on your calendar.
Decide what to stop. Choose at least one task, offer or habit to drop, delegate or simplify.
Set spending limits. Write a budget for [your main expense categories] for the quarter.
## Close the review

Save a one-page summary in [your records folder], share it with [your partner, coach or accountability buddy], and book the date of your next review. Done looks like three goals, a stop list and calendar dates.

title: Back up and protect your data and passwords
purpose: Protects your client information, your money and your work from loss, theft or lockout. Done when your logins are in a password manager, two-step sign-in is on for key accounts, and backups run and have been tested.
tools: Password manager; Cloud storage; External drive; Calendar
steps: ## Take stock
List where your business data lives. Write down your email, [cloud storage], [CRM or contact list], [invoicing tool], computers and phone.
Mark the most important items. Flag client records, financial records, contracts and your own content as the things you cannot afford to lose.
List every business login. Write down each account so none are forgotten when you set up your password manager.
## Protect your logins
Set up a password manager. Move your logins into it and protect it with one strong passphrase of at least [4 unrelated words].
Replace weak and reused passwords. Start with your email, bank and [accounting tool], then work down the list over the next [two weeks].
Turn on two-step sign-in. Do this for your email, bank, [cloud storage] and [CRM], and choose an authenticator app over text messages when you have the option.
Plan for emergencies. Store recovery codes in [a safe place] and write short instructions for [a trusted person] to reach your accounts if you are unavailable.
## Back up your data
Turn on automatic backup for [your computer] and [your phone], and confirm the first backup completes.
Follow a simple rule. Keep [three copies] of important files, on [two kinds of storage], with one copy in a different location.
Export data from tools you do not control. Download contacts, invoices and calendar to [your backup folder] every [month].
Test a restore. Open a file from your backup and confirm it works. Repeat each [quarter].
## Keep it current
Set a reminder for the first day of each [quarter]. Review your tool list, remove access for anyone who has left, and install pending updates.

Check the done list. Done looks like every login in the manager, two-step sign-in on key accounts, backups running and one successful test restore. Check with a [licensed IT professional] if you store sensitive client records.

title: Prepare for tax time and keep records
purpose: Keeps your records organized all year so tax time is calm and your accountant has what they need. Done when your documents are sent, your filing is saved, and next year's dates are on your calendar.
tools: Accounting tool or spreadsheet; Cloud storage; Calendar; Email
steps: ## Set up your record system
Create one yearly folder. Add subfolders for [Income, Expenses, Receipts, Contracts, Mileage and Tax documents] so everything has an obvious home.
Ask your accountant what to keep. Confirm with your [accountant] which records you need and for how long, and write their answer in [your records folder].
Choose a capture habit. Decide that receipts get photographed and filed the same day, using [your phone or scanner].
## Keep records through the year
File receipts weekly. Set a recurring [Friday] reminder to move receipts and bills into the right subfolder.
Keep income records together. Save invoices and matching deposit records in your Income folder as you go.
Track items your accountant asks for. This may include mileage, home office use or equipment purchases, so log them as they happen using [your tracking method].
Save for taxes as you earn. Move [the percentage your accountant recommends] into a separate account each time you are paid, and ask about estimated payment dates.
## Get ready to file
Book your accountant early. Schedule your appointment [6 to 8 weeks] before your deadline and put the deadline on your calendar.
Gather your year-end documents. Collect your profit and loss report, bank statements and [forms you received from clients or platforms].
List the year's changes. Note new hires, equipment purchases, a move, a new offer or a big change in income, so your accountant can ask the right questions.
Send your package securely. Share files through [your secure sharing method] and not as plain email attachments, and answer follow-up questions within [two business days].
## After filing
Save your filed return and confirmation. Put them in your Tax documents folder along with any notice or receipt.

Debrief and plan ahead. Ask your accountant for [two or three] ways to make next year easier, and add next year's deadlines to your calendar. Done looks like documents sent, filing saved and dates scheduled.

title: Ask for a referral
purpose: Turns happy clients into introductions to people who need your help, in a way that feels natural and easy. Done when the ask is sent, the response is tracked, and the person has been thanked.
tools: Email; CRM or contact list; Calendar; Phone
steps: ## Choose the person and the moment
List [5 to 10] people to ask. Pick clients who have had great results, sent a compliment or finished an engagement.
Wait for a good moment. The best time is right after a win, a thank-you note or a milestone, when the value is fresh in their mind.
Decide exactly what you are asking for. Name the kind of person you want to meet, such as [your ideal client description], rather than asking for anyone.
## Make the ask
Write a short, specific message. Thank them, name the result they got, and ask whether they know [type of person] who could use [your service].
Make it easy to pass along. Include a two-sentence blurb they can forward and [your booking link or contact details].
Send it personally. Use a direct email or a call, one person at a time, and not a mass message.
Give an easy way to say no. Add a line such as 'No pressure at all if nobody comes to mind.'
## Follow through
Thank them within [one business day] of any reply, even when the answer is no.
Respond to the introduced person within [one business day]. Mention who suggested you and offer [a first call or free resource].
Update the referrer. Tell them how it went within [two weeks], without sharing private details of the new person.
Log the referral. Record who referred whom in your [CRM or tracking sheet] so you can see where new clients come from.
## Close the loop
Send one gentle nudge after [7 days] if there was no reply, then pause asking that person for [90 days].
Check the done list. Done looks like the ask sent, the reply tracked, the thank-you delivered and the next ask date noted.

title: Collect and use a testimonial
purpose: Captures clear, honest client words and puts them to work in your marketing with permission. Done when you have an approved testimonial saved in your library and published in at least [two places].
tools: Email; Notes document or spreadsheet; Website; Social media accounts
steps: ## Ask for it
Pick your timing. Ask right after a result, a positive comment or the end of an engagement.
Send a request with three simple questions. Ask what was going on before they worked with you, what changed, and who they would recommend you to.
Make replying easy. Offer to take their answers on a [10 minute call] and draft the words for them to edit.
## Get permission
Confirm how you may use it. Ask in writing whether you can share their [name, photo, business name or first name only] and where you plan to use it.
Check the claims. Only share results that are accurate, and check with your [attorney or licensed professional body] if your field has rules about testimonials.
Let them approve the final version. Send the edited text and wait for a clear yes before you publish.
## Put it to work
Edit lightly. Trim to [2 to 4 sentences], keep their voice, and pull out one short headline sentence.
Save it in a testimonial library. Record the text, date, permission and where it is used in [your spreadsheet or notes document].
Publish it in [two or more places]. Good options are your website, your proposals and your social posts.
Thank the client. Send a short note and, if it fits, share where it appeared.
## Keep it fresh
Review your library each [quarter]. Remove anything out of date and note which clients you could ask again.
Honor removal requests. If a client asks to take theirs down, remove it within [two business days]. Done looks like an approved testimonial, saved permission and live placements.

title: Thank and reward a referrer
purpose: Makes every person who sends you business feel seen, so they keep doing it. Done when the referrer has been thanked, rewarded as promised, and kept informed.
tools: Email; CRM or contact list; Calendar; Gift or payment tool
steps: ## Acknowledge the referral
Thank them within [one business day]. Send a personal message by email, text or a call, and say specifically what their introduction means to you.
Log the referral. Record the referrer and the new contact together in your [CRM or tracking sheet] with today's date.
Tell them what happens next. Say you will contact the person and that you will update them in [two weeks].
## Decide and deliver the reward
Check your referral policy. Write down your standard thank-you, such as [a handwritten note, gift of up to [amount], service credit or donation in their name], and what triggers it.
Wait for the trigger. Reward when the referral [books a call, becomes a client or pays], as your policy says.
Check the rules for your field. Some professions limit referral fees or gifts, so confirm with your [attorney or professional body] before you offer money.
Deliver within [5 business days] of the trigger. Add a personal note that names the person's impact and not only the gift.

## Close the loop
Update the referrer on the outcome. Share that the introduction went well and what you did, without private details about the new client.
Add them to your top referrers list. Note their name, referral count and anything they like, in [your CRM or contact list].
Invite them in. Consider a [early access offer, event or private thank-you call] each [quarter] for repeat referrers.
Track costs and results. Record the date, reward and cost in [your referral tracker].

title: Celebrate a client milestone or anniversary
purpose: Marks the moments that matter to your clients so they feel known and want to stay and recommend you. Done when the celebration is sent on the day, logged, and followed by one gentle next step.
tools: CRM or contact list; Calendar; Email; Notes document
steps: ## Set up your milestones
Add key dates to each client record. Include their start date, program completion and goal dates, plus [birthday, if they have shared it].
Choose which milestones you celebrate. A good starting list is [30 days, 90 days, 1 year and goal reached].
Create calendar reminders. Set each one for [one week before] so you have time to prepare.
## Celebrate
Review the client's journey. Read your notes and pick one specific moment, result or effort that deserves a mention.
Choose a gesture. Options include a personal email, a handwritten card, a small gift under [your budget] or a public shout-out with their permission.
Write a personal message. Name the milestone, the specific moment you noticed and what you admire about their progress.
Send it on the day. Keep it short and sincere, and do not attach a sales pitch to the celebration itself.
## Turn the moment into connection
Ask one question. Invite them to share what they are proudest of or what has changed, and listen to the answer.
Offer a next step gently. Mention [your next offer, renewal or resource] in a follow-up a few days later, only if it fits where they are.
Ask for a testimonial or referral only when the moment feels right. Make the request small, specific and easy to decline.
Log it. Record the milestone, what you sent and their response in [your CRM or contact list].
## Check your work
Review your list each [month] for upcoming dates. Done looks like each milestone celebrated on time and each response recorded.
